strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting: detecting biases in the weight space of a linear probe trained on top of a frozen foundation model, initialized from class-name text embeddings, and interpreting the training-induced 'drift' of the weights as evidence of spurious correlations. This differs from prior data-analysis-only approaches (B2T, SpLiCE, Lg) and is a sensible new direction for bias discovery.

The paper evaluates on four standard subpopulation-shift benchmarks spanning two modalities (Waterbirds, CelebA, Nico++, CivilComments), demonstrating generality beyond a single dataset or model type.
A comparison table (Tab. 4) clearly positions the method against existing bias-extraction approaches along fundamental dimensions (bias definition, candidate source, scoring principle).

An ablation (Tab. 2) validates two key design choices (the ranking score and the number of top concepts), and qualitative results (Tabs. 3, 5, 6) allow inspection of extracted biases. The appendix includes a clean proof of the cosine-similarity bound (Eq. 2) and discusses limitations and broader impacts honestly.
weaknesses: The evaluation is indirect and does not directly validate bias identification quality. The main evidence is improved worst-group zero-shot accuracy, but there is no quantitative comparison of extracted biases against ground-truth spurious attributes (e.g., precision/recall of recovered biases on benchmarks with known spurious correlations). It remains unclear how many of the many 'newly discovered' biases (green in Tab. 3) are actually correct versus noise.

Claims of 'significantly improving zero-shot performance' are overstated: the average accuracy drops noticeably on several datasets (Waterbirds 90.7 -> 84.7; CivilComments 83.4 -> 69.0), and only worst-group accuracy improves. The method trades significant average performance for worst-group gains, which is not discussed or analyzed.

The baseline comparison in Tab. 1 is incomplete: B2T and Lg have missing entries on Nico++ and CivilComments, and SpLiCE only on CelebA, weakening the 'over existing SoTA methods' claim. No variance/seeds are reported for any results.

The method is a pipeline of heuristics (YAKE keyword extraction, GIT-Large captioning, WordNet-based hypernym/hyponym filtering, removal of cross-class common keywords) with many ad hoc choices. The concept cut-off (top-q = 15) appears selected post hoc, and the authors explicitly defer a principled cut-off strategy to future work. The filtering step depends on known concept hierarchies, which limits the claimed automation and generality.

The qualitative bias lists raise quality concerns: extracted 'biases' for CelebA include generic or off-topic terms (e.g., 'smiles, woman, long, girl, beautiful' for blonde hair; 'made, hat, brown, eye' for non-blonde), and the paper itself highlights many previous methods' terms as off-topic (red) while including arguably similar noise among its own proposals. Whether weight drift truly isolates spurious attributes versus generic class-discriminative vocabulary is not established.

Novelty relative to the closest prior work (Lg [37], also embedding-space arithmetic on the full dataset) is incremental; the main differentiator is the weight-drift initialization/score, and the ablation shows the score choice only modestly changes results on some datasets (and hurts on CelebA average).

Minor issues hurt polish and credibility: inconsistent naming ('ConceptDrift' vs 'ConceptShift' in Sec. 3.2), duplicate reference [17]/[18], a short main text with much of the substance in the appendix, and no mention of code release, which limits reproducibility of a multi-component pipeline.

strengths: The paper explores a genuinely different angle for bias discovery in foundation models: analyzing the drift of linear-probe weights initialized from class text embeddings, rather than only mining misclassified samples. The motivation that data-level biases need not transfer to model weights is well-argued and supported by the Spawrious example.

Evaluation spans four benchmarks across two modalities (Waterbirds, CelebA, NICO++, CivilComments) with both image and text foundation models (CLIP, mGTE), which is broader than several prior bias-discovery works.

The proposed method consistently improves worst-group zero-shot accuracy over the zero-shot baseline and B2T on the datasets where comparisons exist (e.g., 55.3 vs. 48.1 on Waterbirds; 75.6 vs. 72.8 on CelebA).

The paper includes an ablation on the ranking score and concept cutoff, an appendix with a (simple) formal bound justifying the ranking rule, and an honest discussion of limitations and broader impacts.
weaknesses: The central claim—pinpointing unwanted correlations of the model—is never directly validated. The only quantitative evidence is an indirect proxy (zero-shot prompt augmentation), and the qualitative bias lists (Tab. 3) contain many questionable keywords ('smiles, long, girl, beautiful' for blonde hair; 'made' for non-blonde; 'body' for waterbird). There is no precision/recall against ground-truth spurious attributes, which is available for Waterbirds and CelebA, making the bias-discovery quality claim unsupported.

The evaluation results cut both ways and are not analyzed: average accuracy degrades substantially on Waterbirds (90.7 → 84.7) and CivilComments (83.4 → 69.0), and the reported numbers are internally inconsistent (Nico++ avg 86.2 in Tab. 1 vs. 86.4 in Tab. 2), plus a naming error ('ConceptShift'). Improvements in worst-group accuracy appear to come at an unexamined cost to overall accuracy.

Baseline coverage is weak: several cells are simply missing (B2T on NICO++/CivilComments; SpLiCE and Lg on all but CelebA), so the 'state-of-the-art' claim rests on sparse, partly unreported comparisons, and text-only baselines are absent for CivilComments.

The method is a brittle pipeline whose performance hinges on a captioning model (GIT-Large), YAKE keyword extraction, WordNet filtering, and a hand-picked number of concepts (top-q=15). The ablation shows large sensitivity to these choices (NICO++ worst-group drops from 63.5 to 46.0 with q=30), and the cutoff strategy is explicitly left as future work—effectively a manually tuned hyperparameter.

The claimed key novelty over Lg [37] is thin: both use 'embedding-space arithmetic' on the full dataset (as the paper's own Tab. 4 admits); the differentiator is weight drift, yet the drift itself is never quantitatively characterized or shown to be interpretable beyond the schematic Fig. 1. The theoretical contribution (Eq. 2) is a trivial cosine-similarity bound.
Reproducibility is a concern: no code release is mentioned, the custom NICO++ subset construction and early-stopping details are only briefly described, and key pipeline stages are under-specified.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely interesting and reasonably novel: analyzing the drift of linear-probe weights from class-name embeddings toward spurious attributes is a fresh, weight-space angle on bias identification, contrasting with the prevailing data-analysis (misclassification-based) protocols like B2T.

The method is simple, largely training-free after linear probing, and modality-agnostic in principle; experiments cover both image (Waterbirds, CelebA, Nico++) and text (CivilComments) datasets, which is more scope than most prior bias-extraction work.

Table 1 shows consistent improvements in worst-group zero-shot accuracy over B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg baselines on the datasets where comparisons exist, and the motivation (biases in data need not be biases in the model, per the Spawrious example) is a legitimate and well-argued point.

The paper is clearly written, includes a comparison table of methodological differences (Tab. 4), ablations on the scoring function and concept cut-off (Tab. 2), and the appendix contains the proofs, prompt templates, extracted biases, and dataset setup details.
weaknesses: The central evaluation has a circularity problem: zero-shot accuracy is computed as 'max over templates' per bias, i.e., selecting the best-performing bias prompt per class using test-set accuracy. This is an oracle-style selection, not a deployable protocol, and it likely inflates the reported worst-group gains relative to baselines. It is unclear whether baselines were evaluated under the same selection rule.

Average accuracy degrades substantially relative to the zero-shot baseline (e.g., Waterbirds 90.7 -> 84.7, CivilComments 83.4 -> 69.0). The paper frames worst-group gains as success but does not adequately discuss or justify this large trade-off, especially on CivilComments where the drop is ~14 points.

There is no direct metric for bias-identification quality (precision/recall against known spurious attributes). Claims about 'revealing previously untapped biases' are supported only by qualitative inspection of Tab. 3, where many of the proposed 'new biases' (e.g., 'smiles, woman, long' for blonde-hair; 'made', 'hat'; 'body') look noisy or uninterpretable, weakening the qualitative evidence.

The technical contribution is thin: the scoring (Eq. 3) is a simple cosine-difference, and Eq. 2 is a loose, near-trivial cosine bound. The claim of being 'the first weight-space approach' ignores substantial weight-space interpretability/editing literature, so the novelty claim is overstated.

The core hypothesis that weights 'drift toward biases' is asserted rather than validated; there is no analysis of the trajectory dynamics (e.g., over training epochs) or evidence that drift magnitude correlates with bias strength.

Baseline coverage is incomplete (dashes for B2T on Nico++/CivilComments, missing numbers elsewhere), and suspicious coincidences (SpLiCE and Lg reporting identical 67.2/90.2 on CelebA) plus the 'ConceptShift'/'ConceptDrift' naming inconsistency suggest hasty preparation.

The Nico++ setup is a custom 4-class subset with arbitrary sample counts, limiting comparability to prior work; no code release is mentioned, and sensitivity to the captioning/keyword-extraction pipeline (GIT + YAKE + WordNet filtering), which the authors themselves flag, is not ablated.
Ablation scope is minimal (two variations), and the concept cut-off is left as future work despite the authors showing it materially affects results.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated angle: shifting from data/error analysis to analyzing the drift of the classification layer weights is a genuinely different mechanism for detecting learned spurious correlations, and it does not require counterexamples in validation sets.

Comprehensive multi-modal evaluation: the method is validated on image (Waterbirds, CelebA, ImageNet-1k) and text (CivilComments) datasets, showing breadth beyond typical subpopulation-shift-only works.

Creative and convincing validation for ImageNet: synthetic image generation (FLUX.1-dev) with careful controls (performance on clean generated images on par with original data rules out OOD artifacts), and evaluation across ~100 ImageNet classifiers showing large accuracy drops when the identified SC is present — strong evidence the discovered correlations are actually learned.

Practical utility demonstrated in two ways: an SC-based regularization that improves worst-group accuracy even in a fully spurious setup where GroupDRO degenerates to ERM, and SC-enhanced zero-shot prompting that beats B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg baselines across all tested datasets.

Includes ablations (thresholding strategy, number of candidates, modality gap handling) and an explicit algorithm in the appendix, plus qualitative comparisons of discovered concepts against competitors.

Interesting downstream finding that state-of-the-art ImageNet models (including CLIP ViT-L/14 with 82.4% val accuracy) can be systematically fooled by non-class objects, highlighting a real deployment risk.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a long heuristic pipeline (GIT captioner, YAKE keyword extraction, Llama-3.1 filtering, WordNet post-processing, hand-crafted dynamic thresholding in Eq. 3); the paper provides little analysis of how sensitive the results are to each component, and errors in the pipeline propagate directly into the SC list.

The extracted 'concepts' are often low-quality or nonsensical (e.g., 'kettle kettle kettle kettle', 'man is not a man', 'lime cut' in Tables 13, 16, 17, 21), raising doubts about the precision of the ranking/filtering and about how many of the top-scored concepts are genuinely spuriously correlated vs. noise.

The central mechanistic claim — that drift of final-layer weights toward concept embeddings implies the model has 'learned' the correlation as a decision mechanism — is asserted rather than rigorously established; the linear probe operates on frozen embeddings, so the finding may not transfer to full fine-tuning, and no intervention/causal analysis on the weights themselves (e.g., projecting out SC directions) is provided.

ImageNet validation is limited to only 3 hand-checked scenarios with generated images; the authors themselves acknowledge manual verification was required and that a complete investigation is deferred to future work, so claims about 'previously untapped' ImageNet SCs rest on a small, cherry-pickable sample.

Potential circularity in the fully-spurious-setup experiment: WASP finds the SCs, and the same SCs both define the regularization and (implicitly) the groups on which worst-group accuracy is measured, so the comparison against Lg/GroupDRO may partly favor the method by construction.
Only linear-layer weights are analyzed despite 'weight-space' framing; scalability and applicability to fully fine-tuned or non-linear classification heads is untested.

Some reported gains are modest or mixed (e.g., average accuracy drops on CelebA and CivilComments in Table 5; CivilComments average falls from 80.2 to 71.0), and the method finds no SCs for CelebA-blonde hair, which is attributed to being an 'appropriate decision' but could equally indicate recall issues.
The code link in the abstract is incomplete, and several artifacts (full ImageNet concept lists) are promised only 'upon acceptance', weakening reproducibility in its current form.

strengths: The core idea is genuinely novel: instead of analyzing data distributions or model errors, WASP analyzes the drift of the final classification-layer weights (initialized from class-name text embeddings) in the foundation model's embedding space to identify learned spurious correlations. This is a fresh and interesting angle on SC detection that complements B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg.

The 'fully spurious setup' experiment (Table 3, removing all counterexamples of the SC) is a well-motivated and novel evaluation scenario in which GroupDRO-style methods trivially fail, and the proposed SC-based regularization yields consistent worst-group improvements.

Validation of ImageNet SCs via synthetic image generation (FLUX.1-dev) is creative: showing that adding a detected concept to an image of a correct class flips predictions across ~100 torchvision models (Tables 1, 2, 8-10) provides broad, if indirect, evidence that the identified concepts are genuinely exploited by trained classifiers.

Breadth of evaluation: multiple modalities (image and text), multiple datasets (Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, ImageNet-1k), and multiple downstream uses (regularization, zero-shot prompting), with consistent worst-group gains in Table 5 over B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg.
Ablations (Table 6) on thresholding strategy and modality gap, plus an explicit algorithm and promised code release, aid reproducibility of the core procedure.
weaknesses: The central claim — that weight drift reveals *learned* SCs beyond what validation counterexamples expose — is quantitatively validated on only three hand-picked ImageNet scenarios. The authors concede they 'had to manually ensure that the data is generated correctly' and restricted themselves 'to presenting only a few of our findings.' This leaves the headline ImageNet claim (contribution 3) supported largely by cherry-picked qualitative examples and anecdotal evidence; no precision/recall of WASP's SC detections is ever measured.

The pipeline is a long chain of brittle heuristic components (GIT captioning -> YAKE keyword extraction -> Llama-3.1 filtering -> WordNet post-processing -> ad hoc dynamic thresholding in Eq. 3). Errors in any stage propagate silently, and no analysis is provided of how sensitive the results are to captioner quality, keyword extractor choice, or LLM filtering mistakes. The appendix tables expose this noise directly (e.g., 'kettle kettle kettle kettle', 'limes and limes', 'man is not a man', 'solly').

Concept filtering quality is questionable: many top-ranked 'class-neutral concepts' appear causally or semantically tied to their class (e.g., 'avocado', 'salsa', 'nachos' for Guacamole; 'crochet squares' for Crossword; 'hypocrisy', 'troll', 'hate' for offensive comments). The distinction between 'spurious correlation' and 'plausible co-occurring class evidence' is not rigorously operationalized, weakening the interpretation of several results.

Limited scope of the method: WASP requires a CLIP-like architecture with a text encoder sharing the embedding space of a linear probe over frozen features. It cannot be applied to standard fully fine-tuned classifiers (the many ImageNet models in Tables 2/8-10 are only victims, not analyzable), which narrows the practical reach of a 'weight-space' approach.

Several quantitative gains are thin: on CelebA the worst-group improvement in Table 3 is 9.6% -> 10.4%, and the modality-gap ablation and threshold ablations produce small, inconsistent changes; the dynamic threshold heuristic (Eq. 3) is justified only intuitively with a single figure.

The fairness positioning is defensive and somewhat dismissive: CivilComments is explicitly an identity-bias benchmark, yet the paper disclaims fairness relevance while still reporting on it, without analyzing identity-linked groups.

Statistical rigor is uneven: standard deviations are reported only for the linear-probe experiments; the synthetic-image validation (1000 images per scenario) lacks confidence intervals or significance testing, and the claim that generated images are 'not out of distribution' rests on manual inspection.

Some positioning claims are overstated: 'surpasses all state-of-the-art methods' is not fully supported — comparisons are restricted to B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg on three small datasets, and SpLiCE/Lg have missing entries in Table 5.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated angle: instead of data- or error-based analysis of spurious correlations, WASP analyzes the drift of the linear classification weights relative to their class-name text embeddings, directly targeting *learned* spurious correlations rather than dataset-level correlations that may never affect a classifier.
Broad evaluation across modalities and scales: Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments (text), and ImageNet-1k (1000 classes at scale), which few prior SC-detection methods attempt.

Convincing validation mechanism for ImageNet findings: synthetic images generated with FLUX that clearly depict the correct class while the induced class is absent; extensive Table 1/2 and Appendices B show large accuracy drops (e.g., 100% -> 4.6% for peafowl with firemen) across ~90 ImageNet-trained classifiers, strongly suggesting the discovered correlations are genuinely exploited rather than being generation artifacts.

Practical downstream utility demonstrated: an SC-based regularization that works in a fully spurious (100% correlation, no counterexample) setup where GroupDRO fails (Table 3), and SC-enhanced zero-shot prompting that improves worst-group accuracy over B2T, SpLiCE, and Lg across all three datasets (Table 5).

Includes ablations on the number of selected SCs, dynamic thresholding vs. fixed thresholds, and the text-image modality gap (Table 6), plus a formal algorithm and stated code release, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central mechanistic claim — that classification weights drift *towards* spurious concept embeddings — is asserted rather than directly validated. Fig. 2 is purely illustrative; there is no quantitative trajectory analysis showing that the top-ranked concepts are actually the directions the weights moved along, as opposed to simply correlating with class identity for other reasons.

The method is largely a heuristic pipeline (linear probe + embedding similarity scoring + LLM/WordNet filtering + a hand-crafted dynamic threshold). There is no theoretical justification for the scoring function (Eq. 2) or the thresholding heuristic (Eq. 3), and no ablation on the filtering stage (LLM vs. WordNet vs. none), which is a critical and fragile component.

ImageNet validation is limited to a handful of manually vetted scenarios; the authors admit they 'had to manually ensure that the data is generated correctly' and present only a few findings. This introduces selection bias: it is unclear what fraction of the thousands of discovered ImageNet SCs are genuine versus spurious detections of the method itself. A systematic precision/recall estimate on the discovered SCs is missing.

Possible confound in the synthetic-image evaluation: compositional images containing salient objects like firefighters may shift models' predictions for reasons unrelated to learned spuriousness; the check that base generated images match original model performance is done for only three scenarios, and natural image validation (e.g., retrieval of real photos) is absent.

Results are not uniformly positive: for CelebA blonde-hair, WASP finds no SCs (arguably correct, but also limits evidence of superiority), and average zero-shot accuracy on CelebA and CivilComments actually drops (87.7->85.7, 80.2->71.0 in Table 5), which is not discussed. Some discovered concepts appear noisy or implausible (e.g., 'solly', 'adirondack sitting', 'kettle kettle kettle'), suggesting concept extraction quality issues.

Circularity concern: the same foundation model family (CLIP) is used both as the classifier being probed and as the tool for scoring concepts, so the method may partially measure CLIP's textual semantics rather than the probed model's learned behavior; this is not analyzed.
